simple: your best honest guess of how long work will take, with how sure you are.
analogy: the builders saying "most likely fourteen weeks, almost surely by seventeen".
precise: a statement about the probability distribution of a task's or project's duration or effort, made from the work's content and evidence, independent of what anyone wishes; distinct from a target (a desired date) and a commitment (a promised date chosen as a percentile of the estimate).
source: course definition, F12-23; D1 of F12-23 (Brooks, "The Mythical Man-Month") (pending verification)

simple: three numbers for one task: fast if all goes well, most likely, slow if things go wrong.
analogy: "the walls take two weeks if the weather is kind, three most likely, five if the bricks are late".
precise: a triple (low, likely, high) used as the minimum, mode and maximum of a triangular distribution of a task's duration; its mean (low + likely + high)/3 exceeds "likely" when the high side is longer.
source: course definition and arithmetic, F12-23; run R1 of F12-23

simple: the chain of jobs that decides when the whole project ends.
analogy: foundation, walls, roof, painting: a delay to any of them delays moving in.
precise: for given task durations, the longest path through the dependency graph; any delay on it delays the end by the same amount. Not the critical path of a digital circuit (HW102, HW202).
source: course definition, F12-23; run R1 of F12-23

simple: pretend to run the project thousands of times with random task durations and look at all the finish days.
analogy: building the house ten thousand times on paper, each time with different weather.
precise: repeated sampling of every task's duration from its distribution, computing the project end through the dependency graph for each sample, and reporting percentiles of the end; deterministic when the generator is seeded.
source: course definition, F12-23 (Listing 1, schedule.cpp); run R1 of F12-23

simple: when two paths must both finish before the next job, the later one wins, so waiting for both takes longer than waiting for a typical one.
analogy: the roofers wait for the walls and for the roof tiles, whichever is later.
precise: a task with several predecessors starts at the maximum of their finish times; the expected maximum of uncertain durations exceeds the maximum of their likely values, so single-value plans underestimate every merge point.
source: course definition, F12-23; run R1 of F12-23

simple: how much of the work is really finished, counted by finished pieces.
analogy: counting rooms you can stand in when it rains, not bricks bought.
precise: the sum of the original estimates of tasks whose acceptance test has passed, divided by the sum of the estimates of all known tasks; a simplified form of earned value.
source: course definition, F12-23; runs R3 and R4 of F12-23

simple: learning how wrong your guesses usually are, and correcting for it.
analogy: a builder who knows "my two weeks usually means three".
precise: the distribution of actual/estimate over your own finished tasks, used to scale new raw estimates into a range (median for likely, a higher percentile for a commitment). Not the calibration of a sensor (Calibration, MA202).
source: course definition, F12-23 (Listing 2, calibrate.cpp); curriculum section 19.4 log template (D3 of F12-23) (pending verification)

simple: one way the future could turn out.
analogy: firm ground or soft ground under the foundation.
precise: one member of a set of mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive states of the world relevant to a decision, each with a probability; the probabilities add up to 1.
source: course definition, F12-24; run R3 of F12-24

simple: how good or bad an option turns out in one scenario.
analogy: weeks saved or lost with a shallow foundation on firm or soft ground.
precise: the value of choosing option o when scenario s happens, in one stated unit (for example net team-days); a judgement unless measured, labelled as such.
source: course definition, F12-24

simple: the average result if you could make the same choice many times.
analogy: the weeks a shallow foundation saves on average over many houses on this ground.
precise: EV(o) = sum over scenarios of p(s) times payoff(o, s); the mean of the payoff distribution, which ignores how bad the worst case is. See also Expected value (mean of a distribution), MA202.
source: course definition, F12-24; run R1 of F12-24

simple: how much better you could have done if you had known the future.
analogy: the weeks lost building deep on ground that turned out firm.
precise: regret(o, s) = max over options of payoff(o', s) minus payoff(o, s); the minimax-regret rule chooses the option whose largest regret is smallest.
source: course definition, F12-24; run R1 of F12-24

simple: how much better your decision gets, on average, if you learn something first.
analogy: what the test hole is worth before you dig it.
precise: the expected value of deciding after observing a signal (best option per signal, using Bayes' rule) minus the expected value of deciding now; bounded by the value of perfect information; worth buying only above its cost.
source: course definition, F12-24 (Listing 1, uncertain.cpp); runs R1, R2 and R4 of F12-24

simple: a small, time-boxed experiment that answers one question before a big decision.
analogy: digging a test hole before choosing the foundation.
precise: work whose output is knowledge, not product (a prototype, a load test, a read of a datasheet, a map of callers), with a fixed time budget and a written question; modelled by its cost and accuracy in F12-24.
source: course definition, F12-24

simple: a good choice can turn out badly, and a bad choice can turn out well.
analogy: the storm that damaged a well-built house.
precise: a decision is judged by the information, options, values and reasoning available when it was made (and whether more information was worth getting); the outcome is one draw from the scenarios; a blameless review asks both questions separately.
source: course definition, F12-24

simple: helping someone with less experience grow, mostly by letting them do the work and helping them think.
analogy: the builder who hands the apprentice the trowel.
precise: a voluntary, ongoing relationship in which a more experienced person supports a less experienced person's own goals with questions, examples, feedback and access to experience; the learner owns the goals and the work.
source: course definition, F12-25; D1 of F12-25 (Reilly, "The Staff Engineer's Path") (pending verification)

simple: using your position to open doors for someone.
analogy: the senior builder telling the site lead "let Tariq build the next wall himself".
precise: actions by a person with influence that create opportunities and recognition for another person, as distinct from advice.
source: D1 of F12-25 (Reilly, "The Staff Engineer's Path") (pending verification)

simple: the person who holds the keyboard.
analogy: the one holding the trowel.
precise: in a pair-working session, the person who types and runs commands while the other observes, asks and suggests; in this course's mentoring sessions the learner drives by default.
source: course definition, F12-25

simple: telling someone exactly what you saw in their work, what it caused, and what to try.
analogy: "this joint is wider than the others, so the next row will tilt; check the level every third brick".
precise: feedback that names an observable piece of work, its effect and a concrete next action, about the work rather than the person; the opposite of vague feedback.
source: course definition, F12-25; guide 13.1 (D3 of F12-25)

simple: writing down after each session what happened, what you did, what it caused, and what you will change.
analogy: the builder's notebook each evening.
precise: a short structured note in four parts (what happened, what I did, what effect it had, what I will do next), written by the mentor within a day of a session and read before the next.
source: course definition, F12-25

simple: the rules that keep young learners safe when they work with older ones.
analogy: the site rule that a child apprentice never works alone with one adult behind a closed door.
precise: the policies and practices of a programme that protect learners who are children or vulnerable from harm (where and how sessions happen, who is informed, how messages are exchanged, how concerns are reported); content set by the programme owner and local law.
source: course definition, F12-25; programme rules not yet defined (unverified box in F12-25)

simple: someone who is affected by your work or decides about it, but does not build it.
analogy: the family, the neighbours, the bank that lends the money.
precise: a person or group with an interest in a project's outcome or authority over its scope, time, money or acceptable risk.
source: course definition, F12-26; D1 of F12-26 (Reilly, "The Staff Engineer's Path") (pending verification)

simple: a message whose first sentence says what you need from the reader.
analogy: "we need you to choose by Wednesday" before any pipes are mentioned.
precise: a structure in which the decision or request comes first, then options with consequences, the reason in the reader's terms, evidence and confidence, and finally details.
source: course definition, F12-26 (Figure 1)

simple: a quick label for how a project is doing: fine, worried, in trouble.
analogy: the builders' sign at the gate.
precise: a three-level summary of a project's state against its plan, meaningful only with a rule agreed in advance; in this course earned/planned progress (green at least 0.90, amber at least 0.75, red below), always written as a word with its ratio.
source: course convention, F12-26 (Listing 2, watermelon.cpp); guide 13.6 no meaning by colour alone

simple: a project reported as green on the outside while the data inside is red.
analogy: a house painted outside with no plumbing inside.
precise: a sequence of status reports whose stated colour is better than the colour the team's own data supports (informal term).
source: course definition, F12-26; run R3 of F12-26

simple: describing a technical problem by what it does to the people who care.
analogy: "the kitchen floor goes up one step" instead of "the invert level is too high".
precise: restating a technical fact as its effect on the reader's concerns (users, schedule, money, safety), with the technical fact kept available and unchanged so the translation can be checked.
source: course definition, F12-26

simple: what you owe to the people who depend on your work because you know how it works.
analogy: the electrician who knows what is behind the wall.
precise: the duties that come with specialised knowledge used for others: to the public's safety and well-being, users, colleagues and the organisation, and the profession, set out by professional bodies in codes of conduct.
source: D1 and D2 of F12-27 (ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct; IEEE Code of Ethics) (pending verification)

simple: someone your decision affects who is not part of making it.
analogy: the neighbours, the next family to live in the house.
precise: a person or group affected by a system's behaviour or failure who has no part in its design decisions (bystanders, people recorded by sensors, future maintainers, downstream users).
source: course definition, F12-27

simple: showing only the results that support what you want to say.
analogy: showing the family the one straight wall.
precise: selecting trials, runs, inputs or comparisons for a report because they favour a conclusion, without disclosing the selection; for example the worst run of one version against the best run of another.
source: course definition, F12-27; run R2 of F12-27 (simulated trials)

simple: a public list of the mistakes you published and how you fixed them.
analogy: the letter to the family about the bad cable.
precise: in this university, a log in each chapter's QA record giving date, version, what was wrong, what it now says, the proving source, who found it and which other chapters were checked; corrections are never silent.
source: guide AH-37 to AH-39 (D3 of F12-27)

simple: taking a concern to someone with more authority when the people around you do not act on it.
analogy: calling the family or the inspector when the contractor insists on the thin cable.
precise: raising a documented concern step by step through the organisation's defined path, with facts, risk and options; legal protections depend on the country. Not on-call escalation (Acknowledgement and escalation, SE402).
source: course definition, F12-27; legal details unverified

simple: collecting only the personal data you really need, and keeping it only as long as you need it.
analogy: the builders do not photograph the living room to measure one window.
precise: the design principle of limiting collection, retention and access of personal data to what a stated purpose requires; its legal form depends on local data-protection law.
source: course definition, F12-27; legal details unverified
